source: Schoenfeld (1983) Theoretical and Pragmatic Issues in the Design of Mathematical Problem Solving Instruction (ERIC ED228045)
finding: Schoenfeld says his first problem-solving course taught heuristics plus resource management, with a transfer 'acid test': students must improve on problems unrelated to those taught. A later version passed it 'with flying colors' (cites Schoenfeld 1982). He then says his view of what to teach changed.
numbers: No numbers in this paper for the course gain; it cites Schoenfeld 1982 for the test. Course had 18 students in the construction episode.
quote: the students should show marked improvement on a collection of problems not related to the ones they had studied
limits: Self-report of a course he designed. Numbers live in the 1979/1982 papers, not read here. Early courses were 'cognitive engineering': model the expert, train students to match.
agent_relevance: Transfer was always defined as gain on unrelated problems. Our agent should test heuristics on held-out problem families, not on the ones the prompt was tuned on.

source: Schoenfeld (1983) ED228045, protocol of students on a geometry construction problem
finding: Students who knew the geometry did not reason. They guessed a construction, tried it with compass and straightedge, and repeated. Knowledge was in memory but not used. This is a control failure, not a missing heuristic.
numbers: Typical time 15 to 20 minutes, mostly with tools in hand. 'Not one pair of students reasoned their way to a solution.' Only one pair justified the answer, and only after the fact.
quote: Not one pair of students reasoned their way to a solution.
limits: Qualitative; pairs of students from his own classes; no count of pairs given in the text read.
agent_relevance: Core argument for a control layer: a model may hold the right knowledge and still not call it up. Add a program-level step that forces a check of what is known before trial and error.

source: Schoenfeld (1983) ED228045, section on control behavior and beliefs
finding: Poor monitoring can hurt as much as missing knowledge. Students threw away parts of a solution they already had. Control processes are invisible in textbooks and lectures, so students never see a model of them. His fix: the teacher plays the external manager and asks three questions in class (what are you doing, why, how will it help); this is then handed to small groups and then internalised.
numbers: No effect sizes reported in this paper.
limits: A design proposal with protocol evidence, not a controlled trial. The 'moral' on beliefs is also qualitative.
agent_relevance: The three-question manager maps to a code-driven checkpoint that asks the model: what are you doing, why, what will it give. Keep it triggered by a signal (G1), not by schedule.

source: Sweller, Clark, Kirschner (2010/2011) Mathematical Ability Relies on Knowledge, Too (American Educator, adapted from Notices of the AMS 57(10))
finding: Rival theory: expertise is domain-specific schema knowledge, not general strategy. Authors say Polya-type strategies can be taught but there is no body of randomized controlled experiments showing that teaching them improves problem solving. Novices default to means-ends analysis, which cannot be taught away because it is automatic.
numbers: De Groot chess recall: masters about 70% vs weekend players about 30% on real positions; both about 30% on random positions.
quote: in over a half century, no systematic body of evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of any general problem-solving strategies has emerged
limits: Opinion/review piece, not a meta-analysis; it does not cite Hembree 1992 or Koichu et al. 2007. Strong claim ('no body of evidence') is contestable for specific heuristics like working backward.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the 'knowledge' side is the pretrained model, so heuristic prompts may add little on familiar problem types and more on unfamiliar ones. Measure by problem family.

source: Sweller, Clark, Kirschner (2010/2011) American Educator, worked-example section
finding: The authors propose worked examples interleaved with practice, citing a large body of randomized experiments for the worked-example effect (Sweller and Cooper 1985; Schwonke et al. 2009; Paas and van Gog 2006). They claim there are no separate general strategies that can be learned.
numbers: No effect sizes given in the article; it cites Schwonke et al. 2009 and Sweller & Cooper 1985 for the experiments.
quote: There are no separate, general problem-solving strategies that can be learned.
limits: Worked-example evidence is mostly for novices; the article itself notes this. It argues from absence of RCTs, which is weak against a transfer null that was never tested well.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation to test: does a heuristic prompt help, or does a retrieved worked example of the same type help more? Run both arms.

source: Rott (2015) Rethinking heuristics: characterizations and vignettes (LUMAT 3(1))
finding: Studies of heuristics define the word differently, so coding manuals count different actions. Koichu, Berman and Moore (2007) saw more 'heuristics' after training, but their coding counts metacognitive actions as heuristic. It is then unclear whether training improved strategies, control, or both. Rott's manual excludes metacognition.
numbers: Compares three coding manuals (Koichu et al. 2007, Kantowski 1974, Rott 2012) on the same vignettes; no effect sizes.
quote: the validity of these studies' results is questionable
limits: Conceptual and methodological; it shows how the mixed evidence arises but does not re-estimate effects.
agent_relevance: Explains why 'transfer is mixed': heuristic and control are confounded in most human studies. In our agent, log heuristic operators and control checks as separate events so ablations can split them.

source: Kuzle (2019) Design and evaluation of practice-oriented materials fostering problem-solving competence: working backward (LUMAT 7(3))
finding: Fourteen Grade 5 students got explicit heuristic training once a week (45 min) in a design-research project. Most reversed thinking intuitively at pre-test but struggled with complex reversing tasks. After training the post-test was more homogeneous and every student solved at least one task by working backward correctly.
numbers: N=14. Pre-test: 'Candy task' solved correctly by 11; 'Four gates task' by 3. Post-test: 10 of the pre-test low performers moved to partial or full backward solutions on the harder task; 7 of 12 students improved their working-backward level; only 2 solved both tasks correctly before and after.
limits: No control group, tiny sample, one heuristic, tests not matched in difficulty. Author notes some post-test tasks needed perimeter knowledge not all students had. Transfer to far tasks not tested.
agent_relevance: Gains are local to a single heuristic on near tasks. Teach one operator per problem type with a check that it applied (here: final result recognised as initial value).

source: Kaitera & Harmoinen (2022) Developing mathematical problem-solving skills in primary school by using visual representations on heuristics (LUMAT 10(2))
finding: Finnish fifth graders were taught general heuristics through visual 'Problem-solving Keys' over a school year. Scores on a proportional-reasoning test rose and girls overtook boys. Multiple-choice mixture items did not improve (ceiling).
numbers: N=25 (pre-test 24 scored). Mean 6.1 (SD 2.5) at pre-test to 8.9 (SD 3.6) at post-test, max 14. Girls 5.5 to 9.3; boys 6.5 to 8.4.
limits: No control group, so growth over a school year is not separated from the programme. Same teacher/class, one region, no significance test reported in the passages read. Keys were not available at pre-test but students asked for them at post-test.
agent_relevance: The post-test gain was largest for low scorers. Scaffold for weaker base models, expect small gains at ceiling.

source: Kaitera & Harmoinen (2022) LUMAT 10(2), item-level results
finding: Largest gains were in explaining thinking on an open task, not in easy multiple-choice items. Many students could not describe their strategy at the start.
numbers: Item 6A correct: 6 of 25 (24%) at pre-test, 17 of 25 (68%) at post-test. Answered at all: 17 (68%) pre vs 23 (92%) post.
limits: Same caveats as b08. Difficulty compared to a norm group by the authors' own rating.
agent_relevance: Training helped articulation of method. For an LLM, a required 'state the method' slot may help audits more than accuracy.

source: Kojima et al. (2022) Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
finding: One generic heuristic prompt, 'Let's think step by step', raises accuracy on arithmetic reasoning in large models. It is the weakest possible 'teaching a heuristic' and already moves scores a lot.
numbers: text-davinci-002/InstructGPT-scale: MultiArith 17.7% to 78.7%; GSM8K 10.4% to 40.7% (zero-shot vs zero-shot-CoT). Gains absent on commonsense tasks for some models.
limits: Gain depends on model scale; it underperforms hand-written few-shot CoT. Older models; strong modern models often reason without the trigger.
agent_relevance: Baseline arm for any heuristic scaffold: a scaffold must beat plain step-by-step, not plain direct answer.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Showing worked step-by-step examples (a worked-example intervention, not a heuristic) gives large gains at 540B scale on GSM8K. This is the LLM analogue of the worked-example effect Sweller argues for.
numbers: PaLM 540B GSM8K: standard 17.9% to chain-of-thought 56.9% (+39.0). Other sets: gains of +9.6, +1.8, +10.6, +14.2 on the four other benchmarks in the same row.
limits: Effect appears mostly at large scale (emergent); worked examples were hand-written.
agent_relevance: Supports the rival explanation (b05): worked examples beat abstract strategy text. Compare 'heuristic names' vs 'worked traces' in our ablation.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting
finding: Telling the model to devise a plan, then carry it out (Polya step 2 and 3) beats zero-shot CoT on all ten datasets with GPT-3. Adding detailed instructions (extract variables, compute carefully, PS+) helps more.
numbers: PS+ over zero-shot-CoT: at least +5 points on arithmetic datasets except GSM8K (+2.9). PS average +2.5 over CoT. PS+ average arithmetic 76.7% vs manual few-shot CoT 77.6% and Auto-CoT 75.9%. With self-consistency N=10: GSM8K 73.7% vs 58.7% without; Zero-shot-CoT+SC 70.7%.
limits: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) only. Detailed instructions were tuned on the benchmarks, so the PS+ edge may partly be prompt search. GSM8K gain is small.
agent_relevance: A plan-then-do heuristic is a cheap, reproducible gain on older models. Check on strong current models before trusting it.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting, error analysis (Table 6)
finding: A planning prompt removes few errors of understanding. Semantic misunderstanding stays about the same across methods; missing-step and calculation errors fall slightly.
numbers: 100 GSM8K failures per method. Zero-shot-CoT: calculation 7%, missing step 12%, semantic 27%. PS+: calculation 5%, missing 10%, semantic 26%. Original 46-problem CoT analysis in Fig 1 gave the same three types.
limits: Error shares are of all problems in each sample, hand-labelled by authors; small samples.
agent_relevance: Heuristics tackle step errors, not comprehension errors. Comprehension needs a different operator (restate the problem, check units).

source: Zheng et al. (2023/2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Asking first for the governing principle (abstraction heuristic) then reasoning improves STEM questions, while CoT and 'take a deep breath' do not. Works across three model families.
numbers: MMLU Physics: PaLM-2L 66.4% to 73.2% (+6.8); GPT-4 69.4% to 84.5%; Llama2-70B 51.9% to 64.8%. MMLU Chemistry: PaLM-2L 70.9% to 81.8%. CoT and TDB did not significantly raise PaLM-2L. Five runs each, SD reported.
limits: Baselines shown include 1-shot, CoT and TDB but GPT-4 gains need a comparison to GPT-4 CoT at 82.9% (only +1.6). Principles are in the model's own memory.
agent_relevance: A 'name the principle first' operator is a strong candidate to test, and works for multiple-choice STEM where the failure is picking the wrong rule.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Step-Back Prompting, error and GSM8K analysis
finding: The heuristic fixes a share of baseline errors but adds new ones, and it does not help where principles are trivial. Most remaining errors are in the reasoning step, not in the abstraction.
numbers: MMLU Physics: fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, introduces 11.9% new ones. Over 90% of Step-Back's errors occur at the reasoning step. GSM8K PaLM-2L: baseline 75.8%, Step-Back 84.3%, zero-shot CoT 84.4%, 1-shot 84.5% (no edge over CoT). TimeQA error fix 39.9% vs 5.6% introduced.
limits: Authors' own annotation of errors. GSM8K shows no gain over plain CoT.
agent_relevance: Expect a ceiling: heuristics cannot fix execution. Pair with code-checked computation.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Step-Back Prompting on knowledge QA
finding: Abstraction plus retrieval helps most on hard items. Few exemplars are enough to teach the abstraction skill.
numbers: TimeQA: baseline PaLM-2L 41.5%, GPT-4 45.6%, RAG 57.4%, Step-Back+RAG 68.7%. Hard split: RAG 46.8% to 62.3%. MuSiQue 35.5% to 42.8%; StrategyQA 82.8% to 86.4%. SituatedQA 54.3% to 61%, below GPT-4 63.2%.
limits: Needs retrieval; gain is smaller on SituatedQA and StrategyQA (near ceiling).
agent_relevance: Moderator: gain grows with task difficulty and shrinks near ceiling, as in the human studies.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: The model picks and adapts 'reasoning modules' (a heuristic menu: break into subtasks, critical thinking, etc.) at task level, then follows the structure. It beats CoT and Plan-and-Solve on BBH and agent reasoning, but only modestly on MATH.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: BBH 56 (direct) / 60 (CoT) / 61 (PS) / 67 (Self-Discover); T4D 30/40/42/69; MATH 45/42/49/50.5. GPT-4: BBH 58/75/73/81; T4D 51/52/53/85; MATH 70.5/71/70/73. Wins on 21 of 25 tasks vs CoT. Claims 10 to 40 times less inference compute than CoT self-consistency.
limits: Largest gains on social-reasoning T4D (a task with a clear missing trick); MATH gain is 2 to 3 points on GPT-4. Authors' own benchmark choices.
agent_relevance: Heuristic menu gives big gains when the task needs the right frame, small when the task needs execution. Fits a control layer that picks the operator per task.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover, error analysis on MATH
finding: The self-composed plans are mostly correct but execution fails.
numbers: Structures from PaLM 2-L were correct 87.5% of the time (humans could follow them to solve). 74.7% of failures came from computation errors.
limits: Small manual analysis; the scorer is the authors.
agent_relevance: Structure is not the bottleneck on math. Spend budget on verification of calculations, not on more strategy text.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: Store distilled 'thought templates' from solved problems and retrieve one per new problem (reuse of heuristics as schemas). Large gains on puzzles with a known trick, at much lower cost than tree search.
numbers: Over Meta-prompting: +23% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One. Over GPT-4 baseline Game of 24 +79.4%; over ToT +8.4%. Cost about 12% of multi-query methods on average. Llama3-8B+BoT may exceed Llama3-70B.
limits: Benchmarks have repeated task structure, so template reuse is favoured; the abstract mixes 'over SOTA' with different baselines. Not a human-transfer test.
agent_relevance: Schema retrieval beats re-deriving. Evidence for a library of operators selected by problem type, with caution that tasks are templated.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Prompt the model with Polya's 'do you know a related problem?' to write its own examples before solving. It matches or beats 0-shot and few-shot CoT. Failures show where the heuristic stops working.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: ours about 77.8% vs about 75.0 to 76.7% for 0-shot and few-shot CoT (table text garbled in extraction). Manual check of 100 cases: of 50 correct, 35 had relevant correct exemplars, 9 relevant but wrong solutions, 6 irrelevant. Of 50 wrong, 10 irrelevant, 12 relevant but wrong, 28 relevant and correct yet the model failed (12 generalisation gap, 8 over-reliance on exemplar, 8 other).
limits: Gains are small on GSM8K and larger on MATH and Codeforces; helps only with large-scale models (self-generated examples need competence).
agent_relevance: Model-made analogies can be wrong or misleading. Verify the analogue before using it (G2/G3).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning
finding: Teaching the decompose-then-solve heuristic gives true easy-to-hard transfer where CoT does not. On SCAN length split, CoT on text-davinci-002 collapses to 0.0.
numbers: SCAN length split accuracy: standard 16.7 / CoT 16.2 / least-to-most 99.7 (code-davinci-002); text-davinci-002: 6.0 / 0.0 / 76.0 (100-command subset); code-davinci-001: 0.4 / 0.0 / 60.7. Least-to-most had 13 failures in the test set.
limits: SCAN is a synthetic grammar task with 8-exemplar decomposition prompts crafted for it; transfer is to longer inputs of the same task, not to other task types.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a decomposition heuristic can generalise in length. Test generalisation on harder instances of our items.

source: Suzgun & Kalai (2024) Meta-Prompting: Task-Agnostic Scaffolding
finding: One model acts as conductor, splits the task, calls expert copies of itself, then verifies. Gains over standard, expert and multi-persona prompting across eight tasks, mostly with a Python tool.
numbers: Macro average: meta-prompting (with Python) beats standard prompting by 17.1%, expert (dynamic) prompting by 17.3%, multi-persona by 15.2% (GPT-4).
limits: Without Python it is on par on most tasks and worse on Geometric Shapes. The tool (code) supplies much of the gain. Cost not matched.
agent_relevance: A control layer plus a code tool beats persona prompting. Matches our guardrail G4 against persona voters.

source: Kramer & Baumann (2024) Unlocking Structured Thinking in Language Models with Cognitive Prompting
finding: Prompting with named cognitive operations (goal clarification, decomposition, pattern recognition, generalisation, reorganisation) helps GSM8K for mid-size open models. Gains shrink for larger models that are already near ceiling.
numbers: Six open models, three repetitions on the GSM8K test set. Hybrid CP + few-shot CoT reaches 95% on LLaMA 70B. Qwen 32B high even zero-shot. The exact mid-size numbers are only in figures not readable in the text.
limits: Only GSM8K; only open models; figures, not tables; small reported repetitions; no human baseline. Authors say proportional gain is greater for mid-size models.
agent_relevance: Scaffold value falls as the base gets stronger. Re-measure on our model before keeping each operator.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: GPT-4 labelled math questions with skill names. Retrieving examples by skill label (a skill-based heuristic taxonomy) beat topic-based and generic CoT retrieval.
numbers: MATH: +11.6% over standard CoT, +3.5% over Complex CoT and +3.5% over topic-based. With code, +7.52% over PAL on a 500-item MATH subset (one code example vs PAL's four). +4.0% over CoT with self-consistency.
limits: Skill labels made by GPT-4 on training data; gain depends on exemplar quality; error analysis showed skill errors are only part of failures.
agent_relevance: Choose operators by skill label, not by topic. Requires a labelled bank of past problems.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: The 'check your work' heuristic does not help without outside signal. Earlier positive results used oracle labels. Self-correction can lower accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K: standard 91.5%, self-correct round 1 88.0%, round 2 90.0%; CommonSenseQA 84.0 to 81.5 to 83.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its initial GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and more often turns right into wrong than wrong into right. Self-consistency 3/6/9 responses: 82.5/85.3/88.2 vs 76.7 single (GSM8K, GPT-3.5).
limits: Prompts of the Kim 2023/Shinn 2023 style; stronger recent models or verifier tools may differ.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: a review step must read real output. Self-reflection prompts alone are a known failed transfer from human metacognition teaching.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners (COLM)
finding: Four human-like problem-solving behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) predict whether RL on Countdown works. Priming Llama-3.2-3B with traces showing these behaviours made RL gains match or exceed Qwen-2.5-3B. What matters is the behaviour, not correct answers.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-3B far outperformed Llama-3.2-3B under identical RL. Llama primed with incorrect solutions that still showed the behaviours did about as well as with correct solutions.
quote: models primed with incorrect solutions containing proper reasoning patterns achieve comparable performance
limits: One game (Countdown) and two 3B models; priming data was built with Claude-3.5-Sonnet; the transfer to other domains was shown only through OpenWebMath filtering.
agent_relevance: Heuristic behaviours are teachable to a model, but by training; for a pure scaffold this is evidence that the pattern matters, not the content. Not evidence for prompt-only transfer.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Teaching Algorithmic Reasoning via In-context Learning
finding: Detailed, unambiguous step-by-step algorithm text taught in context (skill, accumulation, composition, tool use) gives out-of-distribution length generalisation. Concrete procedure text works where generic hints do not.
numbers: Error reduction versus best baselines about 10x for long parity, 9x addition, 5x multiplication, 2x subtraction.
limits: Arithmetic and parity only, long hand-written prompts, few-shot with the algorithm shown in full.
agent_relevance: The more concrete the procedure, the better the transfer; vague Polya slogans transfer worse. Operators should be written as exact steps.

source: Schoenfeld (1979) Explicit Heuristic Training as a Variable in Problem-Solving Performance (JRME 10(3))
finding: The founding experiment on explicit heuristic training: trained students were compared with a control on pretest-to-posttest gain and solution procedures. Not read this session: the PDF fetched was damaged and a web fetch timed out.
numbers: not read; do not quote any figure until the paper is opened
limits: Known only from a search snippet. Cited later by Smith 1973 transfer work and by Schoenfeld 1983 as the earlier test of explicit heuristic teaching.
agent_relevance: Priority to open next: it is the origin of the 'teach 5 or 6 heuristics, test near and far' design.

source: Hembree (1992) Experiments and Relational Studies in Problem Solving: A Meta-Analysis (JRME 23(3))
finding: The main meta-analysis of problem-solving research in maths. Not read this session: the host page returned only encrypted script content and ERIC returned no record. Only the aim (assemble all research and condense with meta-analysis methods) was seen in a search snippet.
numbers: not read; do not quote an effect size until opened
limits: Snippet only. It is the check for whether heuristic instruction transfers beyond the taught problems.
agent_relevance: Priority to open next, with Marcucci 1980 and Xin and Jitendra 1999, for effect sizes by instruction type.
